name: Each Breakthrough Is Uncertain
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Engineering Problem or Physics Wall: Two Very Different Kinds of Uncertain
lesson.summary: Not all seven required breakthroughs carry the same kind of uncertainty, some are largely engineering problems likely to yield to sustained investment, while others depend on scientific discoveries that may or may not exist to be found, and confusing the two makes progress sound more assured than the evidence supports.
lesson.body:
The previous two chapters showed why it is so hard to put honest numbers on quantum computing's required breakthroughs, individually or as a bundle. This chapter looks at why the uncertainty itself is not all the same kind of uncertainty, a distinction that matters well beyond quantum computing.

It helps to separate two categories. The first is engineering uncertainty: cases where the underlying physics is already understood, and what remains is refining fabrication techniques, improving materials purity, building better control electronics, or simply investing enough sustained time and money. Problems in this category have a track record of eventually yielding to concentrated effort, the way classical semiconductor manufacturing steadily improved for decades once the underlying physics of transistors was well understood. The second is deep, or fundamental, uncertainty: cases where it is not yet known whether a solution exists at all within known physics or known mathematics, where more funding and more time are not guaranteed to produce an answer because the answer may not be a matter of effort in the first place.

Sorting the seven breakthroughs from this course into these categories is itself informative. Increasing raw qubit count and reducing error rates are generally viewed as closer to the engineering end, difficult and expensive, but without any known physical law standing in the way. Coherence improvements sit closer to the middle, since materials science has produced steady gains for years, but nobody can currently rule out an eventual noise floor set by fundamental physics that engineering alone cannot push past. Connectivity and cryogenics, covered earlier in this chapter's material, involve real physical constraints around heat and wiring density that are not guaranteed to have a purely engineering fix, though nothing known today says they cannot. New algorithms sit furthest from pure engineering: whether a broadly useful quantum algorithm exists for a given real-world problem is a question in mathematics and theoretical computer science, and no amount of funding guarantees that a mathematical discovery happens on any particular schedule, because it might not exist to be discovered, or it might be found by one person on any given afternoon. Cost, discussed earlier, is downstream of all of these, and so it inherits whichever kind of uncertainty the others turn out to have.

This distinction is the real reason to be careful with phrases like "it's basically just engineering at this point." That phrase quietly reclassifies deep uncertainty as engineering uncertainty, making an open scientific question sound like a matter of scheduling and budget. Sometimes that reclassification is accurate. Often, in the more ambitious corners of any emerging technology, it is not, and the difference matters enormously for how much confidence a claimed timeline actually deserves. Learning to ask "is this actually understood physics that just needs refining, or is this still an open scientific question" is a skill that applies far beyond quantum computing, and it is the bridge into the practical toolkit the rest of this course builds toward.
